tip_title: The Term vs. Whole Life Question Has a Simpler Answer Than Most People Think
topic: Life Insurance - Term vs. Whole Decision Framework Revisited
blurb:
💡 **Insurance Tip: The Term vs. Whole Life Question Has a Simpler Answer Than Most People Think**

Most people who feel confused about term vs. whole life insurance are actually confused about one specific thing: what the cash value component in a whole life policy actually does for them day-to-day. Term life covers you for a set window — 10, 20, 30 years — and pays a death benefit if you die in that window. Whole life covers you permanently and builds a cash value account alongside the death benefit, which you can borrow against while you're still alive. The tradeoff is straightforward: term is cheaper and simpler, whole life costs more but doesn't expire. Neither is universally better. The right one depends on what you're trying to solve — a time-limited financial obligation like a mortgage or young kids at home, or a permanent need like final expenses or estate planning.

If you're not sure which one your current policy is, or whether the type you have still fits where you are in life, your Peachy agent can help you think it through — no pressure, just clarity.

📖 [Learn more from Forbes Advisor](https://www.forbes.com/advisor/life-insurance/term-life-vs-whole-life-insurance/)
summary: Covers the functional difference between term and whole life insurance as a decision framework — not a purchase pitch — framed around what problem each type solves, with the cash value mechanic explained plainly. Distinct from the July 27 term-vs-whole tip (general comparison) and Oct 19 tip (cash value mechanics deep-dive) by centering on matching policy type to life stage.
scoring_notes: Life insurance is a consistent high-relevance category across all three audiences, especially East Cobb (established families, empty nesters) and Lewisville Lake (family-heavy). The Oct 19 tip covered cash value mechanics as a standalone explainer; the July 27 tip was a general term-vs-whole comparison. This tip's angle is narrower: matching the TYPE of policy to the problem you're trying to solve (time-limited vs. permanent need), making it a decision-framework framing rather than a mechanics explainer. November is year-end review season, which gives life insurance tips a natural contextual hook. Forbes Advisor is a trusted source. tip_title: November Is When Winter Coverage Questions Actually Matter. Here's What to Check.
topic: Home Insurance - Winter Storm Coverage Readiness
blurb:
💡 **Insurance Tip: November Is When Winter Coverage Questions Actually Matter. Here's What to Check.**

Standard homeowners policies cover a lot of winter damage — burst pipes from a sudden freeze, ice dams that push water through your roof, wind damage from a winter storm. What they don't cover is damage that traces back to deferred maintenance or a heat source you turned off and forgot about. The distinction matters because insurers look hard at the timeline after a cold-weather claim, and "the heat was off for a week" is a fast path to a denied payment. Before the first hard freeze, pull up your declarations page and confirm your dwelling coverage limit still reflects what it would cost to repair or rebuild — construction costs have moved enough in the last few years that a number you set in 2022 might leave you short today.

Not sure if your coverage is set up right heading into winter? Your Peachy agent can walk through it with you — usually takes one quick conversation.

📖 [Learn more from the NAIC](https://content.naic.org/article/consumer-insight-protect-your-home-damaging-winter-weather)
summary: Covers winter storm coverage under standard homeowners policies — specifically what is and isn't covered (sudden freeze damage vs. maintenance-related exclusions) and why November is the right time to confirm dwelling limits before cold weather arrives.
scoring_notes: November publish date makes this highly timely — first hard freezes arrive this month across Georgia and North Texas. Both audiences have meaningful homeowner populations (78% East Cobb, 55% Perimeter, 65% Lewisville Lake). Maintenance-exclusion angle is distinct from the Oct 12 'sudden vs. gradual / pipe freeze' tip, which framed the rule in abstract policy terms. This tip is framed as a concrete November pre-freeze action item with a dwelling-limit check layered in. NAIC is a trusted source.
